extracted.intended_audience: poets, literary readers, and writers seeking criticism or writerly guidance
extracted.subtask_description: Whitman's essayistic reflections that both critique poets (especially Poe and Carlyle) and offer writerly observations about imagery, naming, perception, and what to value in poetry and literary work.

rubrics_metrics.name: Poetical ideal / two shapes of personality
rubrics_metrics.description: “By common consent there is nothing better for man or woman than a perfect and noble life... And yet there is another shape of personality dearer far to the artist-sense... This sort of personality we see more or less in Burns, Byron, Schiller, and George Sand. But we do not see it in Edgar Poe.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Distinguish between (a) the moral, balanced, physically sound ideal in poetry (clear sun, fresh air, eternal moralities) and (b) the artist's preferred personality that delights in strong contrasts, failures, sorrows, and returnings. Evaluate whether a poet/poem aspires to moral exemplarity, to the artistly play of lights-and-shades, or how it negotiates between these ideals (examples: Burns, Byron, Schiller, George Sand vs Poe).

rubrics_metrics.name: Moral principle and democratic/concrete content
rubrics_metrics.description: “Non-complying with these requirements, Poe's genius has yet conquer'd a special recognition... The abnegation of the perennial and democratic concretes at first hand, the body, the earth and sea, sex and the like... and the substitution of something for them at second or third hand...”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Value poetry that grounds itself in immediate, democratic, bodily, and natural concretes (body, earth, sea, sex). Criticize works that substitute second- or third-hand abstractions or excessive technical effects for direct, lived material. Use as an anti-pattern: overly abstracted or second-hand imagery that replaces primary sensory/democratic elements.

rubrics_metrics.name: Technical virtuosity versus emotional heat
rubrics_metrics.description: “Almost without the first sign of moral principle... Poe's verses illustrate an intense faculty for technical and abstract beauty, with the rhyming art to excess... brilliant and dazzling, but with no heat.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess balance between technical skill (rhyme, formal polish, abstract beauty) and felt warmth or moral/emotional substance. A poem may be technically dazzling yet lack 'heat'—emotional vigor, moral weight, or human sympathy—which should lower its evaluation if emotional engagement is a goal.

rubrics_metrics.name: Poetry as cultural diagnostic (reflecting an age)
rubrics_metrics.description: “By its popular poets the calibres of an age, the weak spots of its embankments, its sub-currents... are unerringly indicated.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use poetry to read cultural tendencies and pathologies (e.g., tendencies toward morbidity or abnormal beauty). When evaluating poets or movements, consider what their preoccupations reveal about the era’s 'matter and malady'—not just aesthetic merit but sociocultural diagnostic value.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoiding morbidity/abnormality as a default aesthetic
rubrics_metrics.description: “The lush and the weird that have taken such extraordinary possession of Nineteenth century verse-lovers... The inevitable tendency of poetic culture to morbidity, abnormal beauty—the sickliness of all technical thought or refinement in itself...”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat excessive morbid or 'weird' affect as a suspect trend when it displaces healthy, concrete, or democratic subject-matter. Evaluate whether such affect is a deliberate, meaningful choice or an indulgent technical refinement that substitutes for substance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Title selection: coherence and identifying function
rubrics_metrics.description: “...have a name—something to identify and bind it together, to concrete all its vegetable, mineral, personal memoranda, abrupt raids of criticism... without bothering ourselves because certain pages do not present themselves to you or me as coming under their own name with entire fitness or amiability.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Choose a title that provides identity and cohesion for a collection even if it does not perfectly fit every piece. Prioritize a unifying, evocative name over perfection of fit; a title's role is to bind disparate pieces into a readable whole.

rubrics_metrics.name: Contextual completeness when presenting a scene or work
rubrics_metrics.description: “For really seizing a great picture or book... there comes some lucky five minutes of a man's life, set amid a fortuitous concurrence of circumstances, and bringing in a brief flash the culmination of years of reading and travel and thought... not the great majestic gem alone by itself, but set complete in all its varied, full, indispensable surroundings.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When describing or judging a scene/artwork, account for the surrounding context and circumstances that produce a full apprehension. A powerful impression often depends on a confluence of setting, timing, and prior experience; narratives and criticism should try to situate the object within those 'surroundings' to convey its full impact.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sensory specificity and attention to subtle particulars
rubrics_metrics.description: Examples scattered through the text: the scent of snow, the 'musical low murmur through the pines', 'every snowflake lay where it fell... defined by edge-lines of emerald', 'no two places... exactly alike.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Value and employ precise sensory detail (sight, sound, smell, touch) and moment-to-moment particularity in writing. Such particulars render scenes singular and convincing; avoid generic descriptions that obscure distinctiveness. Use sensory contrasts (noon vs midnight, winter vs summer) to show uniqueness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Attention to performance and technical execution in musical description
rubrics_metrics.description: On Beethoven's septette: 'the band a small but first-rate one... the rendering... by the well-chosen and perfectly-combined instruments... carried away, seeing, absorbing many wonders... to watch the violinists drawing their bows so masterly—every motion a study.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When critiquing musical performance (or describing music in writing), attend to instrumentation, ensemble balance, phrasing, and visible mastery of technique as evidence of interpretive success. Describe how technical execution produces emotional or imagistic effects (e.g., 'soothe and fill me', 'spontaneous, easy, careless').
